title: LNG and Gas Processing Report Review | Cryogenic Weld Data
description: Independent review of LNG and gas processing NDT reports: 9% nickel and stainless weld data, API 620 and 625 tanks, PHMSA Part 193 records, done remotely.
h1: Independent review of NDT reports and inspection data from LNG and gas processing plants
eyebrow: Industry review: LNG and gas processing
intro: LNG facilities are built from materials chosen to stay tough at around minus 162 degrees Celsius, welded with consumables that make ultrasonic examination harder, and regulated by rules that say how long weld records must be kept and how electronic ones must be protected. The inspection records from construction, expansion trains and in-service work therefore carry unusual weight. We review those reports and the digital inspection data behind them, independently, against the codes, the federal rules and the owner's specifications, and set out in writing what the record supports. Reviews are carried out remotely on the files you send.

highlights.p: Nine percent nickel steel, austenitic stainless steel and aluminium each change what a weld report must show, from the technique demonstration to the consumables and penetrant batches recorded.

Where PHMSA's Part 193 applies, the weld examination record is checked against its specific demands, including how long ultrasonic records are kept and how electronic ones are protected from alteration.
TOFD, PAUT and DR files are opened in review software and compared with the report, because coverage and sizing on cryogenic welds can only be confirmed from the data itself.

sections.h: What LNG and gas processing inspection reports cover
p: An LNG value chain produces inspection records at every stage. Gas processing plants treat the feed and recover liquids before it reaches liquefaction; the trains contain cold boxes, heat exchangers, compressors and long runs of stainless and low-temperature piping; storage tanks hold the product; and loading and unloading systems move it to and from ships. Peak-shaving plants and smaller facilities repeat much of that on a reduced scale.

The records that reach us fall into two broad groups. Construction and expansion records establish that welds and materials met the code before the facility entered service, and they are often reopened years later when an operator, a buyer or an insurer needs to rely on them. In-service records track thinning, cracking and insulation problems on equipment whose temperature swings from cryogenic to ambient whenever it is taken down for maintenance.

sections.h: Materials that behave differently at cryogenic temperature
p: LNG equipment depends on materials that keep their toughness at very low temperature. Nine percent nickel steel is widely used for the inner containers of large storage tanks, austenitic stainless steel for piping and many vessels, and aluminium alloys for brazed heat exchangers and some cold-box equipment. Each brings its own welding and examination problems, and a report has to show that it dealt with them.

Nine percent nickel steel is normally welded with nickel-based or austenitic consumables, which leave weld metal with a coarse, oriented grain structure. Ultrasound scatters and bends in that structure, so a technique that performs well on carbon steel welds can lose sensitivity or misplace indications. A credible ultrasonic report on these welds shows that the technique was demonstrated on representative weld samples and that sizing was checked against known reflectors in the same material.

Austenitic stainless welds raise similar ultrasonic questions, and because they cannot be examined by magnetic particle methods, surface examination relies on penetrant testing with materials whose halogen content is controlled. Aluminium welds carry their own penetrant and radiographic practice. The review checks that each report's technique fits the material on the drawing, not the material the contractor usually works with.

sections.h: Storage tanks: API 625, API 620 and Part 193
p: Large LNG storage tanks in the United States are designed and built under a family of documents. API Standard 625 covers tank systems for refrigerated liquefied gas storage as a whole, with detailed container requirements drawn from referenced standards, API 620 and its low-temperature annex among them for metallic containers. PHMSA's LNG regulations in 49 CFR Part 193 incorporate API 620 and NFPA 59A by reference for parts of their requirements.

For tanks with an internal design pressure of 15 psig or less, Part 193 sets ultrasonic examination of the welds to rules drawn from NFPA 59A and Appendices C and Q of API 620, and it attaches record rules to that examination. Ultrasonic examination records must be kept for the life of the facility, electronic records must be held so they cannot be altered, and the ultrasonic equipment must be calibrated at least every eight hours, with suspect welds re-examined if it is found out of calibration. Butt welds in tanks above 15 psig fall under the ASME Section VIII, Division 1 examination rules instead.

Those requirements translate directly into review checks. We confirm that the calibration record shows the required frequency, that any calibration failure led to re-examination of the welds scanned since the last good check, that the stored electronic records are protected from alteration, and that the record set is complete for every seam the tank drawings show.

sections.h: TOFD, PAUT and digital radiography on cryogenic welds
p: Encoded ultrasonic techniques and digital radiography are both common on LNG projects, sometimes on the same weld population. TOFD is valued for detecting and sizing planar flaws through the wall; phased array for covering complex geometry such as nozzles and branch connections; digital radiography for volumetric flaws and for welds where ultrasonic access is poor. Each technique leaves digital inspection data that can be reopened, which is what makes a meaningful review possible.

For TOFD and PAUT, the review checks the scan plan against the weld geometry and the nickel-alloy or austenitic weld metal, the demonstration evidence for the technique, the setup files against the plan, coverage in the encoded data, and the sizing of any recorded indications. For digital radiography, it checks image quality indicator results, signal-to-noise and resolution values against the procedure, the identification of each image to a weld, and any processing applied before interpretation.

Atlantis does not perform industrial radiography in the United States. Film, computed and digital radiography images produced by the owner's licensed radiography contractor are reviewed as documents, and the opinion addresses image quality and interpretation as well as completeness. The ASNT NDT Level III who leads radiographic and ultrasonic reviews also holds certification in MT, PT and VT, so a mixed weld package can be read under one accountable lead.

sections.h: Who regulates LNG facilities, and what they read
p: In the United States, PHMSA sets the federal safety standards for LNG facilities in 49 CFR Part 193, which incorporates NFPA 59A by reference: the 2001 edition for most purposes and the 2006 edition for certain tank provisions. In October 2026 PHMSA released a proposed rule that would move Part 193 to the 2026 edition of NFPA 59A. Until a final rule takes effect, a report is read against the editions currently incorporated, and the opinion says so wherever the distinction matters.

Onshore and near-shore import and export terminals are also authorised by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission under section 3 of the Natural Gas Act, and FERC describes such facilities as remaining subject to its oversight for as long as they operate. FERC and PHMSA coordinate their reviews of LNG projects. We describe that framework in general terms; the operator's regulatory team knows which conditions attach to its own authorisation, and the review reads the record against what they tell us.

Gas processing plants upstream of liquefaction fall under OSHA's process safety management standard where they meet its thresholds, with its documentation requirements for every inspection and test on covered equipment: the date, the person, the equipment identifier, a description of the work and its results.

sections.h: Records that cannot be altered: digital data on LNG projects
p: LNG is one of the few sectors where a federal rule speaks directly to how electronic inspection records are kept. Part 193's requirement that electronic ultrasonic records for low-pressure tanks be retained so they cannot be altered turns a good-practice question into a compliance one. A digital inspection data review asks how that requirement is met in practice: where the raw files live, who can write to that location, whether checksums or write-once storage protect them, and whether the issued digital report can be traced to the exact files it summarises.

Construction projects add digital reporting problems of their own. Weld tracking databases, contractor portals and the owner's document control system each hold a version of the truth, and they rarely agree completely at handover. The review reconciles a sample of welds across those systems, checks that electronic signatures and approval stamps belong to people with the authority and certification to sign, and confirms that TOFD, PAUT and DR files can be opened without the contractor's software licence.
The result is a written statement of how far the digital record can be relied on for the life of the facility, and what should be put right while the people who produced it are still available.

sections.h: Gaps we often find in LNG inspection packages
p: Most LNG packages we see are substantial and well organised. When gaps appear, they tend to be the same ones, and several of them can be closed quickly if they are caught before the contractor demobilises.
list: Ultrasonic procedures demonstrated on carbon steel blocks and then applied to nickel-alloy weld metal without further demonstration
Calibration checks recorded at the start of a shift but not at the frequency the rule or procedure requires
Penetrant batch certifications missing for work on austenitic stainless welds
Encoded scans that stop short of the weld length on the drawing, or that cannot be linked to a seam number
DR images with image quality values below the procedure's requirement, accepted without comment
Weld counts in the tracking database that do not match the number of examination records
Electronic records stored in project folders that any user could edit

p: Atlantis does not review reports for projects where it performed the examination, and discloses any relationship with the contractor at the enquiry stage. Members of the review team come from oil and gas, petrochemical, nuclear and maritime work. Eddy current data on exchanger tubes, and any other technique outside UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, are assigned in the proposal to a reviewer holding the certification your contract requires.

Fitness-for-service and remaining-life assessments stay with the operator's engineer; we do not perform them. The inspector of record, and any approval that rests with the regulator or the owner's own inspection authority, stays where it is. The review is carried out remotely from Houston and Hyderabad on records shared through a secure transfer, which suits projects whose documents are spread across the owner, the EPC contractor and several NDT companies.

faqs.q: Can you review ultrasonic weld records for 9% nickel tank shells?
faqs.a: Yes. We check that the technique was demonstrated on representative nickel-alloy weld metal, that calibration was recorded at the required frequency, that coverage in the encoded data matches the seams on the drawings, and that indications were sized by a method the procedure supports.

faqs.q: Does Part 193 affect how ultrasonic records are kept?
faqs.a: For tanks with an internal design pressure of 15 psig or less, it requires ultrasonic examination records to be kept for the life of the facility and electronic records to be retained so they cannot be altered. The review checks how the records are actually stored, not only what the report says about them.

faqs.q: Do you review radiographs and DR images from LNG construction?
faqs.a: Yes. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, but film, CR and DR images produced by your licensed contractor are reviewed for image quality, identification, coverage and interpretation.

faqs.q: Which NFPA 59A edition do you read the report against?
faqs.a: The edition Part 193 incorporates for the provision concerned, unless your authorisation or specification says otherwise. Because PHMSA has proposed moving to a newer edition, the opinion states which edition it applied wherever the difference matters.

faqs.q: Can you review records from a gas processing plant that feeds an LNG facility?
faqs.a: Yes. Thickness surveys, amine unit cracking surveys, weld records and process safety inspection documentation from gas plants are reviewed against API 510, API 570, the relevant damage mechanisms and the plant's own procedures.

faqs.q: Can a review help at project handover?
faqs.a: Yes. A handover review reconciles weld counts between the tracking database and the examination records, checks that the digital files can be opened and are protected, and lists what should be corrected while the contractors are still mobilised.

faqs.q: Can you review in-service records after a cold spot or insulation finding?
faqs.a: Yes. The review checks how the thermal survey finding was followed up, which areas were opened or examined, whether the technique suited the material and its temperature history, and whether the follow-up covered the whole affected area.

faqs.q: How do I request an LNG report review?
faqs.a: Use the form on this page or write to info@atlantisndt.com describing the asset, the weld or equipment population, the methods and the decision the review supports. We reply within one business day with a scope and a quote; the files then reach us through secure transfer.
